questionText: `public abstract class BeverageMaker { public void boilWater(){ System.out.println("Boiling water"); } public abstract void brew(); public void pourInACup(){ System.out.println("Pouring in a cup"); } public abstract void addCondiments(); public void makeBeverage(){ boilWater(); brew(); pourInACup(); addCondiments(); } }`. Which method is the actual "Template Method" here?
option1: boilWater()
option2: makeBeverage()
option3: brew()
option4: addCondiments()
correctOptionExplanation: makeBeverage() defines the fixed algorithm skeleton/sequence; the rest are individual steps -- some fixed (boilWater, pourInACup), some deferred to subclasses (brew, addCondiments).

questionText: In the same BeverageMaker class, which methods are steps subclasses are required to fill in, versus fixed for every beverage?
option1: All four methods must be overridden by every subclass
option2: boilWater() and pourInACup() must be overridden; brew() and addCondiments() are fixed
option3: None of the methods can be overridden anywhere
option4: brew() and addCondiments() are abstract and must be implemented by every subclass; boilWater() and pourInACup() are concrete, fixed steps identical for every beverage
correctOptionExplanation: brew() and addCondiments() have no default implementation and must be supplied by each subclass; boilWater() and pourInACup() are already complete and behave the same for every beverage.

questionText: `class CoffeeMaker extends BeverageMaker { public void brew(){ System.out.println("Coffee"); } public void addCondiments(){ System.out.println("adding sugar to my coffee"); } } BeverageMaker coffee = new CoffeeMaker(); coffee.makeBeverage();`. Exact order of console output?
option1: Boiling water, Coffee, Pouring in a cup, adding sugar to my coffee
option2: Coffee, Boiling water, adding sugar to my coffee, Pouring in a cup
option3: Boiling water, Pouring in a cup, Coffee, adding sugar to my coffee
option4: adding sugar to my coffee, Coffee, Boiling water, Pouring in a cup
correctOptionExplanation: This is a direct readout of makeBeverage()'s fixed sequence: boilWater, brew, pourInACup, addCondiments.

questionText: `public abstract class PaymentProcessor { public abstract IPayment createPayment(); private void validate(double amount){ if(amount <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Amount must be a positive number"); } private void logTransaction(double amount){ System.out.println("this amount was transacted " + amount); } public boolean requiresOTPVerification(){ return true; } private boolean verifyOTP(){ return true; } public void processOrder(double amount){ validate(amount); if(requiresOTPVerification()){ boolean otpOK = verifyOTP(); if(!otpOK){ System.out.println("OTP verification failed"); return; } } IPayment payment = createPayment(); payment.pay(amount); logTransaction(amount); } }`. validate(), logTransaction(), and verifyOTP() are all private. Yet processOrder() calls all three successfully for every subclass. Why does this work?
option1: Private methods are secretly treated as public by the JVM at runtime
option2: processOrder() is actually generated separately for every subclass, with its own private copies
option3: Private access only restricts visibility to code outside the class -- it says nothing about one private method calling another within the same class; since processOrder() lives inside PaymentProcessor itself, it can call validate(), logTransaction(), and verifyOTP() freely regardless of which subclass the actual object is
option4: validate(), logTransaction(), and verifyOTP() are implicitly converted to protected the moment a subclass exists
correctOptionExplanation: Privacy is a visibility boundary around the class, not a restriction on the class's own internal calls. processOrder() and the private helpers all belong to PaymentProcessor, so they can call each other freely.

questionText: Can CardPaymentProcessor call validate(amount) directly, or override it to add a card-specific minimum-amount rule?
option1: Yes to both -- validate() is inherited like any other method
option2: No to both -- private members are not inherited or visible to subclasses at all; CardPaymentProcessor can't call validate() directly, and writing a method named validate(double amount) in CardPaymentProcessor wouldn't override anything -- it'd just be an unrelated new method
option3: It can call it, but not override it
option4: It can override it, but not call it directly
correctOptionExplanation: Private members are invisible to subclasses entirely -- no calling, and no overriding, just an unrelated same-named method if you try.

questionText: Someone, confused, writes this inside CardPaymentProcessor: `public class CardPaymentProcessor extends PaymentProcessor { private void validate(double amount){ if(amount < 10) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Card payments need at least 10"); } public IPayment createPayment(){ return new CardPayment(); } }`. What actually happens when processOrder() runs on this object?
option1: Compile error -- you can't redeclare a private method from the parent
option2: CardPaymentProcessor's new validate() silently replaces the parent's for this instance
option3: Java merges both validate() methods and runs whichever throws first
option4: Nothing changes -- processOrder() (defined in PaymentProcessor) still calls PaymentProcessor's own private validate(), completely unaware CardPaymentProcessor has an unrelated private method with the same name. This is method hiding, not overriding -- a classic private-method trap
correctOptionExplanation: Since validate() is private, PaymentProcessor's processOrder() always calls PaymentProcessor's own validate(). CardPaymentProcessor's method of the same name is just a separate, unrelated method that happens to share a name.

questionText: In the actual code, processOrder() is not marked final. What real risk does that create?
option1: A subclass could override processOrder() entirely -- skip validate(), reorder the OTP check, drop logTransaction() -- completely defeating the point of having a fixed recipe
option2: No risk at all, since processOrder() only calls private methods
option3: The code won't compile until processOrder() is marked final
option4: final only applies to fields, not methods, so this is a non-issue
correctOptionExplanation: Without final, any subclass can override the template method itself and rewrite or skip the fixed sequence, which defeats the entire purpose of the pattern.

questionText: What's the correct fix to guarantee no subclass can ever change the sequence in processOrder()?
option1: Mark PaymentProcessor itself final
option2: Make processOrder() private
option3: Declare it public final void processOrder(double amount) { ... } -- still callable by clients, but impossible for any subclass to override
option4: Remove processOrder() from PaymentProcessor and copy it into every subclass
correctOptionExplanation: public final keeps the method usable by client code while locking its implementation against being overridden -- this is exactly how you take the 'rule' away from the child and give it to the parent.

questionText: requiresOTPVerification() is public, returns true by default, and is not abstract. What's this called in Template Method terms, and how does it differ from createPayment()?
option1: It is an abstract method just like createPayment() -- identical role
option2: It is a hook method -- it has a default implementation, and subclasses may optionally override it to influence the template's behavior; createPayment() is a required abstract step every subclass must implement, with no default
option3: It is a constructor
option4: It is a private helper unrelated to the algorithm
correctOptionExplanation: Hooks provide a sensible default and are optionally overridden; abstract steps provide no default and must be implemented by every subclass.

questionText: `public class CashPaymentProcessor extends PaymentProcessor { public IPayment createPayment(){ return new CashPayment(); } @Override public boolean requiresOTPVerification(){ return false; } }`. When new CashPaymentProcessor().processOrder(500.0) runs, what's different compared to CardPaymentProcessor?
option1: processOrder() runs a completely different method body for CashPaymentProcessor
option2: validate() is skipped for cash payments
option3: logTransaction() is skipped for cash payments
option4: The if(requiresOTPVerification()) check evaluates false, so the whole OTP block is skipped -- everything else (createPayment(), pay(), logTransaction()) runs exactly as normal
correctOptionExplanation: Overriding the hook only affects the one conditional branch it controls; every other fixed step in processOrder() runs unchanged.

questionText: A new NetBankingPaymentProcessor needs to be added. Following this codebase's pattern, what's the minimum required?
option1: Create NetBankingPayment implements IPayment with its own pay(), then NetBankingPaymentProcessor extends PaymentProcessor implementing createPayment() to return it -- nothing in PaymentProcessor needs to change
option2: Add a new else if branch inside processOrder() for net banking
option3: Modify IPayment to add a payViaNetBanking() method
option4: Rewrite PaymentProcessor from scratch, since a new payment type is fundamentally different
correctOptionExplanation: OCP applies to Template Method just as it does to Strategy -- a new subclass implementing the existing abstract step is purely additive.

questionText: createPayment() is abstract and returns an IPayment that the rest of processOrder() then calls .pay() on. What does this detail reveal about the design?
option1: This is pure Template Method with no other pattern involved
option2: IPayment makes this a Singleton Pattern
option3: createPayment() acts as a Factory Method -- a well-known variant where the subclass-filled step specifically creates an object -- nested inside the larger Template Method (processOrder()); patterns get combined like this constantly in real code
option4: This turns the whole design into the Strategy Pattern instead
correctOptionExplanation: The abstract 'step' here is specifically an object-creation step, which is exactly the Factory Method pattern, used as one ingredient inside the larger Template Method.

questionText: Both Template Method and Strategy Pattern let you vary one piece of behavior while keeping the rest fixed. What's the actual mechanical difference?
option1: No real difference -- same pattern, different names
option2: Template Method varies behavior through inheritance -- which steps run is locked in the moment you pick a concrete subclass and can't change without creating a different object; Strategy varies behavior through composition -- an injected object can be swapped via a setter on the same instance at runtime
option3: Strategy always requires abstract classes; Template Method always requires interfaces
option4: Template Method can only ever have one subclass; Strategy allows unlimited implementations
correctOptionExplanation: Template Method fixes behavior at the class-hierarchy level (compile time, per subclass); Strategy fixes behavior at the object-composition level (swappable at runtime).

questionText: You want to add an optional addIce() step to BeverageMaker for cold drinks, but CoffeeMaker and TeaMaker don't need it at all. What's the correct approach so they need zero changes?
option1: Make addIce() abstract, forcing CoffeeMaker/TeaMaker to implement an empty version anyway
option2: Add an if (beverageType.equals("cold")) check inside makeBeverage()
option3: Delete addIce() entirely since not everyone needs it
option4: Give addIce() a default no-op body in BeverageMaker (a hook, same idea as requiresOTPVerification()), call it from makeBeverage(), and only override it in the specific subclasses (e.g. IcedCoffeeMaker) that need it
correctOptionExplanation: A no-op default hook lets only the subclasses that care override it, while every existing subclass is completely unaffected.

questionText: You want CardPaymentProcessor to enforce a ten rupee minimum while CashPaymentProcessor allows any positive amount -- without making validate() itself overridable. Clean way to do this?
option1: Keep validate() as the fixed private step, but have it call a new overridable hook like protected double minimumAmount() { return 0; } for the threshold; CardPaymentProcessor overrides just minimumAmount() to return 10, while validate()'s enforcement logic itself stays untouched and un-overridable
option2: Make validate() public and let every subclass override it entirely
option3: Remove validate() from the template and call it manually inside each subclass's createPayment()
option4: Hardcode if (this instanceof CardPaymentProcessor) inside validate()
correctOptionExplanation: This isolates exactly the one varying number (the threshold) behind a small hook, while the actual enforcement logic (throwing when amount is below the threshold) stays fixed and safe inside validate().

questionText: `public abstract class BeverageMaker { public abstract void brew(); } public class CoffeeMaker extends BeverageMaker { private void brew(){ System.out.println("Coffee"); } }`. What's wrong with this?
option1: Nothing, this compiles and works exactly like the original
option2: brew() needs a return type of void[]
option3: Compile error -- Java doesn't allow overriding a method with a more restrictive access modifier; brew()'s contract in the parent requires at least public visibility, so dropping it to private in the override is illegal
option4: abstract methods can never be overridden at all
correctOptionExplanation: Java forbids narrowing visibility when overriding -- an override must be at least as accessible as the method it overrides.

questionText: Why might a fixed step like logTransaction() be declared protected final instead of private, if you still never want it overridden?
option1: protected final and private behave identically in Java
option2: protected final lets subclasses (or others in the hierarchy) call the method directly if genuinely needed, while final still guarantees no subclass can ever override or change its behavior -- controlled visibility without giving up control of the logic
option3: protected final methods are automatically treated as abstract
option4: protected methods can be overridden but private ones can't, so this makes no sense as a choice
correctOptionExplanation: protected final is the combination that grants visibility to the hierarchy while still locking the implementation against being changed.

questionText: `public class TeaMaker extends BeverageMaker { @Override public void makeBeverage(){ brew(); addCondiments(); } public void brew(){ System.out.println("tea"); } public void addCondiments(){ System.out.println("adding lemon to my tea"); } }`. Assuming makeBeverage() is NOT marked final in BeverageMaker, is this valid, and what does it mean for the pattern?
option1: Invalid -- Java doesn't allow overriding a concrete method
option2: Invalid -- brew()/addCondiments() can't be called from an overridden makeBeverage()
option3: Valid, and this is the intended way to customize behavior in Template Method
option4: Valid Java, but it defeats the whole purpose -- TeaMaker has escaped the fixed recipe that was supposed to belong to the parent, exactly the failure final exists to prevent
correctOptionExplanation: Without final, nothing stops a subclass from replacing the entire template method and skipping steps -- which is exactly what happened here (boilWater and pourInACup got dropped).

questionText: Four subclasses (C1, C2, C3, C4) share steps f1(), f2(), f3() from a common parent. C1/C2/C3 are all fine running them in the same fixed order (say f3 then f1 then f2), but C4 genuinely needs a fundamentally different order for its business logic. Correct approach?
option1: Define a second template method (e.g. process2()) in the parent (or a related abstract class) with C4's required order, and have C4 use that one instead of trying to break the first template method's final lock
option2: Remove final from the first template method so C4 can override and reorder it freely
option3: Force C4 to somehow work with the same order even though its logic doesn't support it
option4: Duplicate all of f1/f2/f3's logic directly inside C4 instead of extending the parent at all
correctOptionExplanation: One final template method per fixed recipe -- a genuinely different recipe gets its own template method, not a broken lock on the first one.

questionText: You need CardPaymentProcessor (and only CardPaymentProcessor) to run a fraud-risk check before validate() even runs, without touching processOrder()'s existing behavior for every other processor. Cleanest fix?
option1: Copy processOrder() into CardPaymentProcessor and add the fraud check at the top
option2: Make validate() protected instead of private so CardPaymentProcessor can wrap it
option3: Add a new hook to PaymentProcessor, e.g. protected void beforeProcessing(double amount) {} with an empty default body, call it as the very first line of processOrder(), and override it only in CardPaymentProcessor -- every other subclass is unaffected since the default does nothing
option4: Add an if (this instanceof CardPaymentProcessor) check inside processOrder()
correctOptionExplanation: Before/after hooks bracketing the fixed algorithm are a standard Template Method extension -- empty-by-default, overridden only where actually needed.

questionText: You want CashPaymentProcessor's OTP requirement to depend on the amount -- skip OTP under 500, require it above. Can a hook method take parameters like requiresOTPVerification(double amount)?
option1: No, hooks must always be parameterless like the current requiresOTPVerification()
option2: Yes -- a hook is just a regular method with a default implementation; protected boolean requiresOTPVerification(double amount) { return true; }, called as requiresOTPVerification(amount) from processOrder(), is perfectly valid and lets CashPaymentProcessor make an amount-dependent decision
option3: No, because processOrder() cannot pass its local variables into any method it calls
option4: Yes, but only if the hook is also marked abstract
correctOptionExplanation: A hook is just a method with a default body -- it can take parameters exactly like any other method, and the template method decides what to pass in.

questionText: A developer "optimizes" PaymentProcessor by caching the OTP result in a field instead of a local variable: `public abstract class PaymentProcessor { private boolean otpOK; public void processOrder(double amount){ validate(amount); if(requiresOTPVerification()){ otpOK = verifyOTP(); if(!otpOK){ return; } } IPayment payment = createPayment(); payment.pay(amount); logTransaction(amount); } }`. Why is this riskier than keeping otpOK as a local variable?
option1: It isn't riskier -- fields and locals behave identically here
option2: It would cause a compile error since abstract classes can't have fields
option3: It changes processOrder()'s return type
option4: If the same PaymentProcessor instance is ever reused for multiple orders concurrently (shared across threads, or re-entered), one call's otpOK could be overwritten by another call in progress, corrupting both -- a local variable is scoped to a single invocation and can't leak across calls the way a field can
correctOptionExplanation: Instance fields persist and are shared across every call on that instance; a local variable is private to each individual method invocation, which is what you want for per-call intermediate state.

questionText: PaymentProcessor gains a second template method for refunds: `public final void refundOrder(double amount){ validate(amount); IPayment payment = createPayment(); logTransaction(amount); }`. Can refundOrder() reuse the exact same private validate() and logTransaction() that processOrder() already uses?
option1: Yes -- both template methods live in the same class as those private helpers, so both can call them freely, avoiding duplicated validation/logging logic
option2: No, each template method needs its own separate private helpers
option3: No, a private method can only ever be called from one calling method in its class
option4: Yes, but only if both template methods are marked final
correctOptionExplanation: Private just means 'only this class can call it' -- it doesn't restrict how many methods within that same class are allowed to call it.

questionText: createPayment() is currently abstract. A teammate proposes giving it a default instead: `public IPayment createPayment(){ return new CashPayment(); }` so subclasses can optionally skip overriding it. What's the trade-off?
option1: No trade-off, strict improvement
option2: Compile error, since PaymentProcessor is abstract
option3: Flexibility goes up (a subclass forgetting to override it won't fail to compile), but correctness safety goes down -- a subclass that genuinely needs its own payment type could silently fall back to cash processing with no compiler warning; the abstract version forces a deliberate, explicit choice
option4: This makes createPayment() a hook that must always be overridden
correctOptionExplanation: Turning a required step into a hook trades a compile-time safety net for convenience -- a real design trade-off, not a free win.

questionText: Every current and planned PaymentProcessor subclass needs to reject any amount over a hard system-wide cap of one lakh rupees -- this exists purely to catch data-entry typos like an extra zero, and there is no case where any subclass would want a different cap. What's the right way to add this check?
option1: Add a new hook like protected double maxAllowedAmount() { return 100000; } that every subclass could theoretically override
option2: Add the cap check directly inside the existing fixed, private validate() -- since every subclass needs identical behavior with zero variation, there's nothing to make overridable; adding a hook here would just be unnecessary indirection
option3: Make validate() abstract so every subclass implements its own cap check
option4: Add the check inside createPayment() instead, since that's already abstract
correctOptionExplanation: Same discipline as the OCP/ISP 'don't abstract what never varies' lesson -- hooks exist for genuine per-subclass variation, not to decorate logic everyone needs identically.

questionText: PaymentProcessor now has two independent hooks: requiresOTPVerification() (default true) and a new requiresFraudCheck() (default true). CashPaymentProcessor overrides only requiresOTPVerification() to return false. A new TrustedPartnerProcessor overrides only requiresFraudCheck() to return false. Do these hooks interfere with each other?
option1: Yes, overriding one automatically overrides the other since they're in the same class
option2: No, because only one hook can be active per subclass
option3: Yes, CashPaymentProcessor would also skip fraud checks as a side effect
option4: No -- each hook independently gates its own section of processOrder(); CashPaymentProcessor still runs the fraud check (default true), TrustedPartnerProcessor still runs OTP verification (default true) -- they compose without either needing to know the other exists
correctOptionExplanation: Independent hooks are exactly that -- independent. Each one only controls the branch it's checked in, regardless of what other hooks exist.

questionText: Both CardPaymentProcessor and UPIPaymentProcessor need OTP verification enabled -- exactly the default. Should either override requiresOTPVerification()?
option1: No -- the parent's default (return true;) already matches what both want, so there's nothing to override; only CashPaymentProcessor, which genuinely differs, should override it
option2: Yes, every subclass should explicitly override every hook for clarity, even to repeat the default
option3: Yes, otherwise requiresOTPVerification() would return false for them by default
option4: No, because a hook can only ever be overridden by exactly one subclass in the whole hierarchy
correctOptionExplanation: Overriding a hook just to repeat the default is pure duplication -- only override where behavior actually needs to differ.

questionText: Product wants timing instrumentation logged for every processOrder() call, across all payment types. Compared to adding the same instrumentation in a Strategy-Pattern design (each payment type as a separately injected strategy, no shared method wrapping all of them), what's Template Method's practical advantage here?
option1: No advantage, both designs require identical effort
option2: Because every subclass's behavior is funneled through the one fixed processOrder() in the parent, timing can be added by editing that single method once -- every subclass gets it automatically; a pure Strategy design without a shared context method would need each strategy (or the calling code) adjusted individually
option3: Template Method makes timing instrumentation impossible since methods are private
option4: Strategy Pattern automatically includes timing instrumentation, so this is a non-issue there
correctOptionExplanation: Template Method centralizes control flow in one place, so cross-cutting changes that apply to everyone only need to be made once, at the parent.
